evidence.excerpt: In the meantime, when his time came, burst forth from the egg without (the help of his) mother, Garuda of great splendour
that mighty being endued with strength, that bird capable of assuming at will any form, of going at will everywhere, and of calling to his aid at will any measure of energy.
And all the deities seeing him, sought the protection of Vibhavasu (Agni). And they bowed down to that deity of manifold forms seated on his seat and spake unto him these words
He is the mighty son of Kasyapa, the destroyer of the Nagas, engaged in the well-being of the gods, and the foe of the Daityas and the Rakshasas.
thou art the very Hiranyagarbha; thou art the progenitor of creation in the form of Daksha and the other Prajapatis
thou art Indra (the king of the gods), thou art Hayagriva the steed necked incarnation of Vishnu
thou art the arrow (Vishnu himself, as he became such in the hands of Mahadeva at the burning of Tripura)
thou art the four-faced Padmaja; thou art the Brahmana (i.e., wise), thou art Agni, Pavana, etc. (i.e., the presiding deity of every object in the universe).
thou art Brahma without attributes
At the sight of the splendour resembling that of Yama when in wrath, our hearts lose all equanimity and quake.
Sauti said, 'Then hearing of and beholding his own body, that bird of beautiful feathers diminished its size.'
the controller along with the Rishi wended their way towards Garuda and adored him of birds
Saunaka said, 'When did the revered Surya resolve at the time to burn the worlds? What wrong was done to him by the gods that provoked his ire?'

when Rahu was drinking nectar among the gods at the time of the churning of the ocean he was pointed out to the gods by Surya and Soma, and from that time he conceived an enmity towards those deities.
Rahu sought to devour his afflictor (Surya)
Then the gods, accompanied by the Rishis, wended to the Grandsire, and said unto him
The intelligent son of Kasyapa is known to all by the name of Aruna.
I have told thee now why Surya was in wrath, and how Aruna, the brother of Garuda, was appointed as his charioteer.
Sauti continued, 'Aruna, at the behest of the Grandsire, did all that he was ordered to do.
Thither lived Vinata in affliction, defeated in wager and put into a state of slavery.

Once Kadru calling Vinata who had prostrated herself before the former, addressed her these words in the presence of her son, 'O gentle Vinata, there is in the midst of the ocean, in a remote quarter, a delightful and fair region inhabited by the Nagas. Bear me thither!' At this that mother of the bird of fair feathers bore (on her shoulders) the mother of the snakes.
And thereupon the snakes, scorched by the rays of the Sun, swooned away. And Kadru seeing her sons in that state prayed to Indra, saying
I bow to thee, thou slayer of Vritra! I bow to thee, thou slayer of Namuchi!
O thou of a thousand eyes, consort of Sachi!
O Purandara, thou art able to grant rain in torrents.
Thou art Vayu (the air), the clouds, fire, and the lightning of the skies.
Thou art the light of all creatures, Aditya, Vibhavasu, and the wonderful elements.
And then Indra, the king of gods, having the best of horses for his bearer, thus adored by Kadru, covered the entire firmament with masses of blue clouds.
That island had been fixed by the Creator of the Universe as the abode of the makaras.
And they commanded the lord of birds, viz., Garuda, of great energy
Garuda, alter reflecting for a few moments, asked his mother Vinata, saying, 'Why, mother, have I to do the bidding of the snakes?'
Vinata said, 'O thou best of birds, I have become, from misfortune, the slave of my co-wife.
Let Marut (the god of the winds) protect thy wings
A certain Brahmana with his wife had entered the throat of that ranger of the skies.
Unto Garuda who had thus addressed him that Brahmana said, 'O, let this woman of the Nishada caste, who is my wife, also come out with me.'
And then that Brahmana, accompanied by his wife of the Nishada caste, came out, and praising Garuda wended whatever way he liked.
He then saw his father, and, hailed by him, Garuda, of incomparable prowess made proper answers. And the great Rishi (Kasyapa) then asked him

Kasyapa replied, 'This lake thou seest is sacred. It hath been heard, of even in the heavens. There is an elephant, with face downwards, who continually draggeth a tortoise, his elder brother. I shall speak to you in detail of their hostility in former life. Just listen as I tell you why they are here.
There was of old a great Rishi of the name of Vibhavasu. He was exceedingly wrathful. He had a younger brother of the name of Supritika.
The latter was averse to keeping his wealth jointly with his brother's. And Supritika would always speak of partition.
But as thou, Supritika, without regarding my advice impelled by desire of separation, always wishest to make an arrangement about your property, thou shall become an elephant.
Supritika, thus cursed, then spake unto Vibhavasu, 'Thou also shall become a tortoise moving in the midst of the waters.'

unresolved: The Vibhavasu reference in Kadru's hymn on physical page 35 is retained provisionally. This passage does not securely identify it with Agni/Vibhavasu or the Rishi Vibhavasu.

This batch does not establish identity among Hiranyagarbha, Padmaja, Brahma without attributes, the Grandsire, and the Creator of the Universe. The hymns' statements equating Garuda or Indra with numerous beings do not establish interchangeable personal identities.
This batch does not explicitly establish identity among Pavana, Vayu, and Marut, or between Aditya and Surya.
The shared spouse implied by Vinata's co-wife statement is unnamed. Its connection to Kadru is contextual, and this batch does not identify that spouse with Kasyapa.
The possessive in 'in the presence of her son' on physical page 35 is ambiguous; it does not securely establish an additional individual distinct from Garuda or support a parent_of claim for Kadru.
Kadru's snake sons remain an undifferentiated group in this batch; no individual children are identified for parent_of records.
The singular Rishi accompanying the gods is retained provisionally because the physical page 34 sentence is grammatically disrupted. The passage does not securely establish that Rishi's identity.

Vibhavasu is explicitly a Rishi in the former-life account and is subsequently identified with the lake's tortoise; Supritika is identified with its elephant. These animal forms are recorded in descriptions rather than treated as additional individuals or personal-name aliases.

matches.reason: Corroborated by parentage from Kasyapa and Vinata, the title lord of birds, and overlapping page 34 descriptions of his abilities.
Both records cite the same page 34 passage explicitly identifying Vibhavasu as Agni, whom the frightened deities approach.
Both records identify him as Garuda's parent through the same page 34 statement; the current account additionally calls him Garuda's father.
Corroborated by motherhood of Garuda and the continuing story of her enslavement after the wager with Kadru.
Both passages specifically place Daksha among the Prajapatis in the context of creation.
Corroborated by the explicit title king of the gods, control of downpours, and the Purandara invocation naming his victories over Vritra and Namuchi.
Both records associate Surya with Vinata's offspring as his charioteer and with Soma's exposure of Rahu during the nectar episode.
The existing record explicitly identifies Ugrasrava as Sauti; the current Sauti continues the same framing narration to Saunaka concerning the nectar episode and Garuda.
Corroborated by his framing role as Sauti's questioner in the continuing discussion of the ocean-churning narrative and its consequences for Surya.
Both accounts describe Rahu drinking nectar among the gods, being exposed by Surya and Soma, and subsequently seeking to swallow Surya.
Both records identify Soma as Surya's companion in exposing Rahu while he drinks nectar among the gods.
Corroborated by her motherhood of the snakes and the continuing wager-and-slavery story involving Vinata.
Both records identify Vritra as the opponent slain by the figure addressed as Indra or Purandara.
Both records name Namuchi as slain by the figure addressed as Purandara, alongside Vritra.
